newsitem.title: EGYPT: Cairo bourse needs new issues to perk up - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Cairo bourse needs new issues to perk up - analysts.

text.p: Jittery investors are abandoning Egypt's stock market, which needs new issues and a shake-up of its infrastructure to end the downtrend in force since March, analysts and brokers said on Monday.

The Capital Market Authority (CMA) all-share index hit its lowest level since late January, closing 1.63 points down on Monday at 348.37 points -- a far cry from the record high of 427.77 reached on February 24.
At first brokers said the decline was an overvalued market correcting itself.

Later they attributed the continuing drops to capital-flush foreign investors slinking away to other regional markets, where price-to-earning ratios were below the high 17 and 18 levels the Egyptian market had reached.

But they have since started pointing fingers at the government and the CMA for their lack of urgency on privatisation, which has encouraged investors to dump their shares and foreigners quietly to withdraw.

"The bourse is boring; foreign investors are bored and disappointed with the pace of the privatisation programme. They don't want to trade the same stocks; the market needs broadening," said Patrick George, a Middle East analyst at London-based securities house HSBC James Capel.
Egypt's accelerated economic reform programme, with privatisation as its backbone, is one of the lures the government has cast to draw in foreign investment.

In January 1996 Egypt appointed a new cabinet steered by Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri and it has since moved from merely talking about privatisation to actually selling majority stakes in its corporate holdings.
But in spite of grandiose official promises to privatise scores of firms before, by and after the middle of the year, the state has sold equity stakes in only about 11 firms since March.
"The money is there. The investors are willing but where are they going to put it? They are waiting for the promised firms," said Hany el-Beltagi at El-Rashad Securities Brokerage.

"The companies offered are already listed and those that weren't scared off investors because they took a long time to process, their offer prices were too high or investors were just not interested," he added.

They are so uninterested, brokers say, that the market did not even perk up after the International Finance Corporation said it would include the Egyptian index in its composite investable index from November.
Wobbly bourse infrastructure has also helped drive clients away from the Egyptian stock exchange, the brokers say.

Shireen ElKady, chief investment officer at analysts Prime Investments, bemoans the lack even of an automatic matching system to coordinate buying and selling, while London-based brokers complain about the bourse's clearing system, which takes several days to process transactions.

Average volume, which is the market pulse, is now about 50 million pounds ($15 million) a day, below the 60 million pounds during the market's heyday. "What the market needs is time, market makers and a solution to the critical issue of settlements," said Mark Campbell at international securities firm T. Hoare and Co.
But in spite of the gloom and doom, brokers predicted the market does not have long to go before bottoming out.
With time, they say, it will escape these temporary doldrums as the country's solid economic reputation and its sound market fundamentals bode well for the future.
"Egypt is still a favourite among emerging markets," said George. "We recommend this market and now it's attractive."
As the market matures, institutional investors will replace the more nervous individuals who shed their holdings at the first sign of trouble, creating a much-needed balance, they add.
"The market is very healthy and people should not be fooled by this downtrend," said Mohammed Abdalla, managing director of brokers Intercapital.
"Things can't go up indefinitely, that's what investors need to know. There's no panic and these extremes are natural in any emerging market. It will go up eventually." $ = 3.386 (Egyptian Pounds)
